item.title: Six Mocktails: Coconut, Citrus, a Not-a-Mule, and Three for the Beach
item.description:
Six no-alcohol drinks. The first three cover different ground — creamy/tropical, bright/citrus, ginger-forward. The second three (watermelon mojito, virgin paloma, mango chili-lime) were picked to travel: each adds just one new bottle to the cooler and reuses lime, mint, agave, and soda already on the list below, rather than needing its own dedicated shopping trip. No expertise assumed on my end either — these are straightforward builds, not bartending theory.

Tools and stock worth having on hand

  • Cocktail shaker (or any lidded jar/container that seals — a mason jar works)
  • Jigger or a set of measuring shot glasses (1 oz / 2 oz)
  • Citrus juicer or reamer — fresh juice matters a lot more than bottled here, especially for lime
  • Muddler (the back of a wooden spoon works in a pinch) — for mint
  • Fine strainer, if shaking anything with pulp or muddled mint
  • Copper mugs, if leaning into the mule presentation — not required, just traditional
  • Full-fat coconut milk (canned, not the carton beverage) and coconut water are different ingredients below — don’t swap one for the other
  • A bottle of good non-alcoholic ginger beer (strong ginger bite, well-carbonated) and a bottle of club soda or seltzer
  • Agave syrup (or 1:1 agave-and-water simple syrup) — shared by the citrus spritz, the paloma, and the mango chili-lime below
  • Coarse salt or Tajín, for rimming glasses — one small shaker covers the paloma and the mango chili-lime

Packing these for the 5-hour drive down

This is a drive to a beach house with its own kitchen and freezer, not a cooler-only day trip — so the plan is simpler than packing for a walk to the sand:

  • Ice and blending both happen on arrival, not in the car. No need to haul ice down — the house has a freezer, and the blender/muddler work is easiest done in an actual kitchen anyway.
  • Bring whole watermelons and mangoes, not pre-juiced bottles. Whole fruit travels fine at room temperature for 5 hours and blends better fresh at the house than juice that’s been sitting since before you left — this also skips worrying about fresh watermelon/mango juice oxidizing or losing flavor over the drive, which was a real concern for pre-blending, and isn’t one for whole fruit. Bottled watermelon juice or mango nectar are still fine fallbacks if you’d rather not deal with a whole watermelon at all.
  • Pre-mix the chili-lime salt in a small shaker or travel container (or just bring a bottle of Tajín) — no different whether you’re rimming a glass at home or at the beach house.
  • Cans of soda/ginger beer over open bottles — they hold carbonation better over a long drive and don’t go flat if the trip is bumpy.
  • Fresh lime, grapefruit, and blood orange juice travel fine for 5 hours if juiced ahead and kept in the car’s AC rather than a hot trunk; agave, salt, and canned coconut milk don’t need any special handling at all.

Coconut Colada

Creamy and tropical — the coconut mocktail to reach for over a piña colada. Full-fat canned coconut milk gives real body; coconut water alone comes out thin.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 2 oz full-fat coconut milk (canned, shaken well first)
  • 3 oz pineapple juice
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • Splash of club soda or sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Garnish: pineapple wedge or wheel, mint sprig

Method: Shake the coconut milk, pineapple juice, and lime juice hard with ice — the coconut milk wants the agitation to emulsify and get that piña-colada texture. Strain into a glass over fresh ice, top with a splash of soda, garnish.

Variation: swap the club soda for a splash of ginger beer if you want more spice against the coconut.

Source: Be Well Table — Pineapple Coconut Mocktail.

Blood Orange Citrus Spritz

Bright and a little tart — blood orange juice has more depth than regular orange juice, and the color is the best-looking drink of the three if blood oranges are in season (roughly winter into early spring in most US markets; regular orange juice works fine off-season, just less dramatic).

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz blood orange juice (fresh-squeezed if you can get blood oranges; bottled is fine otherwise)
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 0.5 oz agave syrup or simple syrup, to taste
  • Sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Garnish: orange wheel or twist

Method: Combine the juice, lime, and agave in a glass over ice, stir, then top with sparkling water. No shaking needed — this one’s built, not mixed.

Source: One Lovely Life — Blood Orange Mocktail.

The Not-a-Mule

A Moscow mule’s whole appeal is ginger heat against lime and fizz — none of that depends on the vodka, so dropping it loses less than you’d think. This is the one worth serving in a copper mug if you own them; the cold-metal thing is real, not just presentation.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 4 oz good non-alcoholic ginger beer (strong ginger, well-carbonated — the quality of the ginger beer is the whole drink here)
  • 0.75–1 oz fresh lime juice
  • Splash of club soda, optional, for extra fizz if the ginger beer alone isn’t lively enough
  • Ice
  • Garnish: lime wheel, mint sprig

Method: Fill a copper mug (or any glass) most of the way with ice. Add lime juice, top with ginger beer, stir gently — stir, don’t shake, or the ginger beer goes flat. Top with a splash of club soda if you want more sparkle. Garnish and serve immediately.

Source: Yummy Mummy Kitchen — Virgin Moscow Mule, Whisk Affair — Virgin Moscow Mule.

Watermelon Mojito (beach house-ready)

Reuses the lime and mint already on the list, plus club soda you’re already packing for the Not-a-Mule. The only new item is a whole watermelon — bring the fruit itself and blend at the house, rather than pre-juicing for the drive.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz watermelon juice (blended fresh from the whole fruit and strained, or bottled if you’d rather skip the blender entirely)
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 4–5 mint leaves
  • Club soda or sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Garnish: mint sprig, watermelon wedge

Method: At the house — cube the watermelon, blend, strain out the pulp if you want a cleaner drink. Muddle the mint gently in the bottom of a glass, add lime juice and watermelon juice, fill with ice, top with soda, stir once.

Source: The Merry Thought — Watermelon Mojito Mocktail, The Real Food Dietitians — Watermelon Mojito.

Virgin Paloma (beach house-ready)

Same lime juice and agave as the Blood Orange Citrus Spritz, same sparkling water as everything else on this page — the only new bottle is grapefruit juice.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz grapefruit juice (fresh-squeezed if you’re juicing at home the night before; bottled is fine)
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 0.5 oz agave syrup, to taste
  • Sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Salt (or Tajín) for the rim
  • Garnish: lime or grapefruit wedge

Method: Rim a glass with lime juice and dip in salt or Tajín, combine grapefruit juice, lime juice, and agave over ice, top with sparkling water, stir.

Source: Sweets & Thank You — Virgin Paloma, Mingle Mocktails — Paloma Mocktail.

Mango Chili-Lime (beach house-ready)

Reuses the lime, mint, and salt/Tajín already on the list — a whole mango (or bottled mango nectar, if you’d rather skip peeling and pureeing one) is the one new thing to bring.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz mango puree (blended fresh from a whole mango) or mango nectar
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 3–4 mint leaves
  • Sparkling water or club soda, to top
  • Ice
  • Chili-lime salt (Tajín, or your own chili/salt/sugar mix) for the rim
  • Garnish: lime wedge, mint sprig

Method: Rim the glass with lime juice and chili-lime salt, same as the paloma. Muddle or tear the mint into the glass, add lime juice and mango puree, fill with ice, top with soda, stir.

Source: Aura Bora — Mango Chili Lime Mocktail, Whole30 — Mango-Chili-Lime Mocktail.

item.title: Dog Biscuits: Pumpkin and Peanut Butter
item.description:
A simple, crunchy dog biscuit with five ingredients and no mixer: whole wheat flour, pumpkin, peanut butter, and eggs. Makes about 3 dozen 2-inch biscuits.

Two label checks before you start.

  • Peanut butter must have no xylitol. Xylitol (sometimes labeled “birch sugar”) is toxic to dogs. Plain peanut butter with just peanuts and maybe salt is the safe choice; check the label even on brands you trust.
  • Pumpkin must be 100% pure puree, not pumpkin pie filling. Pie filling has sugar and spices (nutmeg is harmful to dogs in quantity).

Ingredients

Amount Ingredient
2½ cups whole wheat flour, plus more for dusting
½ cup 100% pure pumpkin puree
¼ cup natural peanut butter, xylitol-free (unsalted if you can)
2 large eggs
½ tsp ground cinnamon (optional)
2–4 tbsp water, only if the dough is too dry

Equipment

  • Large bowl and a sturdy spoon
  • Rolling pin
  • Cookie cutter (about 2 inches), or a knife or pizza wheel for squares
  • Parchment-lined baking sheets

Method

  1. Heat the oven to 350°F. Line two baking sheets with parchment.
  2. Mix the wet ingredients. In the bowl, whisk the pumpkin, peanut butter, and eggs until smooth. Stir in the cinnamon if using.
  3. Add the flour a little at a time, stirring until a stiff dough forms. If it is crumbly and won’t come together, add water a tablespoon at a time; if it is sticky, work in a little more flour.
  4. Roll it out on a floured surface to about ¼ inch thick. Cut out biscuits and set them on the sheets, close together; they don’t spread.
  5. Bake 20–25 minutes, rotating the sheets halfway, until the biscuits are firm and the edges are lightly browned.
  6. Dry them out for a crunchier biscuit: turn the oven off and leave the biscuits inside for 1–2 hours, or until hard. Cool completely on a rack.

Storage

  • Airtight container at room temperature for up to 1 week (they are drier and last longer if you did the oven-off step).
  • In the refrigerator for up to 2–3 weeks.
  • In the freezer for up to 3 months.

Notes

  • Treat these as treats, not a meal. As a rule of thumb, treats should be no more than about 10% of a dog’s daily calories.
  • If your dog has a wheat or egg allergy, or you’re not sure these ingredients are right for them, check with your vet first.
  • Skip raisins, chocolate, onion, garlic, and xylitol in any variation of this recipe; all are harmful to dogs.
  • For a wheat-free version, swap in oat flour (or ground rolled oats) and expect a slightly crumblier dough; add a little extra flour if it is sticky.

item.title: Converting a Threaded SodaStream/Drinkmate to a 5 lb CO2 Tank
item.description:
Swapping the tiny 14.5 oz cylinder that ships with a threaded (screw-in) SodaStream or Drinkmate for an external 5 lb tank — same carbonation, without buying $15–20 exchange cylinders every 60 liters.

This only applies to screw-in machines. The connection depends on the TR21-4 thread — the “blue label” screw-in cylinder standard shared by classic SodaStream machines and Drinkmate. SodaStream Terra and Art use a push-in quick-connect cylinder and are not compatible with this approach — they need a different adapter, if one exists at all. Confirm your machine actually screws the cylinder in before buying anything.

The core idea: no regulator

The stock 14.5 oz cylinder feeds the machine unregulated, at something like 850 psi (CO2 tank pressure is a function of temperature, not fill level, until the tank runs dry — so a “full” 5 lb tank and an almost-empty one both sit around the same pressure at a given room temperature). The machine’s own trigger valve is what meters gas into the bottle in short bursts; it’s designed for that pressure already.

That means the standard approach is a direct adapter hose — CGA320 (the tank’s valve standard) on one end, TR21-4 (the machine’s cylinder thread) on the other — with no separate pressure regulator in between. Adding a regulator dialed down to, say, 130 psi would just give weaker carbonation than stock, not a safety improvement; the machine already expects full cylinder pressure.

Parts

  • 5 lb aluminum CO2 cylinder, CGA320 valve. Aluminum over steel — lighter, won’t rust internally. Buy new, not refurbished, DOT-approved with a current hydro-test date (5 lb aluminum cylinders in the US are DOT-3AL, hydro-tested every 5 years; the date’s stamped on the collar and a gas supplier will check it before filling or exchanging). VEVOR and Beverage Elements both make commonly-recommended 5 lb aluminum CGA320 cylinders.
  • CGA320 → TR21-4 direct adapter hose, 36–60 in, braided stainless or reinforced food-grade hose, rated well above tank pressure (most listings claim 4500–5000+ psi, which is the hose/fitting rating, not an indication you need that much pressure). Get one with a gauge and bleed valve — the bleed valve lets you depressurize the line before disconnecting, which matters (see below). Grab spare nylon washers/o-rings while you’re at it.
  • Tank strap or wall bracket. A pressurized 5 lb cylinder becomes a genuine projectile hazard if the valve gets sheared off in a fall — secure it upright, always. Upright also isn’t optional for a different reason: these adapters pass gaseous CO2 only. A tipped tank can send liquid CO2 into the machine, which the setup isn’t built for.

Tools/consumables: adjustable wrench, a spray bottle of soapy water for leak-checking every threaded joint, spare washers.

Where to buy

Cylinder — buy local if you can. A welding or beverage-gas supplier will sell a 5 lb aluminum cylinder and fill it on the spot with beverage-grade CO2, and you skip shipping a pressure vessel entirely. If ordering online, the VEVOR 5 lb aluminum CGA320 cylinder is the commonly-recommended budget option; homebrew retailers like MoreBeer and Williams Brewing carry better-vetted tanks and are reputable for this whole category.

Adapter hose:

Product Notes
Soda Helper Universal CO2 Adapter Hose (OmniFizz/Aarke Carbonator 3), 60" Low-profile hose rather than a metal-shell braided one — won’t scratch counters. Spare washers included.
Soda Helper CO2 Adapter Hose & Base Kit for OmniFizz Same hose plus a machine base — tidier countertop setup.
GURUDAR CO2 Direct Adapter, 60" stainless Listing explicitly names DrinkMate compatibility. Label warns gaseous CO2 only, tank upright.
Tiiyee CGA320 → TR21-4 with gauge and bleed valve, 60" The gauge + bleed valve combo is worth having over a bare hose.

Other reputable non-Amazon sources for the hardware in general: MoreBeer, Williams Brewing, Soda Dispenser Depot, or a local welding/gas supply shop for the tank itself.

Gas purity

An in-line filter is not the real control here, and a cheap one won’t reliably catch what actually matters: industrial and welding-grade CO2 can carry compressor oil and hydrocarbon residue that a basic filter doesn’t remove. Two things that do the real work:

  1. Specify beverage-grade / food-grade CO2 at the fill counter, every time — not the general-purpose industrial tank.
  2. Buy a new cylinder, so you’re not inheriting rust or residue from whatever the tank held in a past life.

An activated-carbon in-line gas filter from a homebrew supplier is a reasonable belt-and-suspenders addition, but largely redundant if the gas source is clean — and check its pressure rating before adding it to this unregulated, full-tank-pressure line, since most are speced for regulated low-pressure use downstream of a proper regulator.

Safety notes

  • The cylinder is the real hazard, not the gas connection. Standing, strapped, away from heat and direct sun. A cylinder is not a countertop decoration — treat it like the pressure vessel it is.
  • CO2 displaces oxygen. It’s heavier than air and pools low in a room. This is a real risk for any large-volume leak, not just a slow one — don’t store or operate the tank in a small closed cabinet with no airflow, and if you ever smell/hear a active leak, ventilate before troubleshooting.
  • Bleed the line before disconnecting. The gauge/bleed-valve hose exists specifically for this — open it to vent residual line pressure before you unscrew anything, rather than cracking a pressurized fitting open by hand.
  • Leak-test every threaded joint with soapy water after assembly — bubbles mean it’s not sealed.
  • Don’t overtighten the TR21-4 end. The washer does the sealing, not torque.
  • Drinkmate’s own warranty generally doesn’t cover damage from third-party CO2 sources — know that going in.

Before you order

  • Confirmed the machine is screw-in (TR21-4), not the push-in quick-connect used on SodaStream Terra/Art
  • Cylinder ordered/sourced: new, aluminum, CGA320, current hydro-test date, filled with beverage-grade CO2
  • Adapter hose ordered: CGA320 → TR21-4, with gauge and bleed valve if available
  • Tank strap or bracket sourced and installed before the tank goes anywhere near the counter
  • Every joint leak-tested with soapy water on first hookup

item.title: Barrel Sauna Roof and Porch Plan
item.description:
Plan for an Almost Heaven four-person cedar barrel sauna with an electric heater. Goals: stop rain drips through knots and seams, add insulation for cold-weather heating, and add a covered spot to change at the door.

Note: This is general building guidance gathered from Almost Heaven’s own roof suggestions, product listings, and common practice. It is not from the Almost Heaven manual, so confirm key details with Almost Heaven or a sauna builder before committing. Product and spec claims were checked against public listings on 2026-11-04 (see Verification notes); anything still unconfirmed is marked unverified.

Quick expectations

  • Cedar swells when wet, so small drips through knots and seams are common. A roof greatly reduces them but may not eliminate them. Almost Heaven itself says some seepage is normal.
  • Do not caulk or foam the tongue-and-groove joints. The wood moves with heat and moisture, and rigid fill will crack or split boards.
  • Keep some airflow at the roof edges so moisture can escape. Trapped moisture causes mold and rot.
  • In 30°F weather, expect a longer preheat, often 60 to 90 minutes (a rule of thumb, not a measurement). A roof with insulation helps more than sealing gaps, though the ends, door and floor still lose heat.
  • Heater: 4-person Almost Heaven barrels are commonly listed with a 6 kW Harvia (some Watoga listings show 4.5 kW; the larger Essex lists 8 kW on a 240 V, 40 A hard-wired circuit). Check the label on your own heater and put it on a dedicated circuit; have an electrician confirm the wiring.

The plan in pictures

The three diagrams below cover the whole job. Layer thicknesses are exaggerated, and the barrel dimensions are placeholders until you measure yours.

Roof options from Almost Heaven’s guidance

  1. Removable canvas rain jacket. Easiest, clips on with bungees, can stay on while the sauna is running, and Almost Heaven sells one (listings show roughly $245 to $280). It is a cover and not insulation. Cheap, reversible first step.
  2. Corrugated metal roof screwed on with short (about 3/4 inch) sheet metal screws. Their staves are 1-3/8 inch thick, so short screws are safe going straight into the staves.
  3. Roofing shingles over underlayment, covering as much of the top as you like.
  4. A full shelter or structure with a roof.

Recommended build: insulated roof over the barrel

From the inside out:

  1. Barrel staves (existing cedar, 1-3/8 inch).
  2. Insulation strips. Rockwool Comfortboard 80, 1.5 inch (R-4.2 per inch, so about R-6.3), cut lengthwise into strips roughly 4 to 6 inches wide and laid along the barrel like extra staves. At that width a flat strip sits within about 1/8 inch of a 6 ft diameter curve, so the board does not need to bend. Stagger the end joints. Buy one pack first and test the fit.
  3. Furring strips running around the curve (over the top from one side to the other, like hoops), spaced about 1 foot apart. They hold the insulation down and give the roof something to fasten to. Use thin, bendable strips, or rip quarter-inch plywood into narrow strips.
  4. Underlayment (roofing felt or synthetic), which keeps the mineral wool dry.
  5. Roof surface: corrugated metal or shingles, with a drip edge at the bottom so water sheds clear. Corrugated panels need to be curved with the ribs running around the barrel; shingles follow the curve more easily.

How it is fastened (this corrects the first draft, which only mentioned short screws):

  • Furring to staves: the screw has to pass through the furring and the insulation, so use about 3 inch screws (3/4 inch furring + 1.5 inch insulation + about 3/4 inch into a 1-3/8 inch stave). Pre-drill, and test on a spare stave or a hidden spot so the tip does not reach the sauna interior.
  • Roof to furring: 1 to 1-1/4 inch roofing screws with washers that stop in the furring. The original 3/4 inch screws are Almost Heaven’s advice for fastening metal straight to the staves, not through a furring layer.

Cautions:

  • Mineral wool loses insulating value when damp, so the underlayment and roof edges must shed water cleanly.
  • Account for the steel hoops on the barrel. The flat strips and furring can ride over them; confirm they sit flat.
  • Wear gloves, eye protection and a dust mask when cutting mineral wool; use a serrated blade.
  • Unverified: I could not find a Rockwool maximum service temperature for Comfortboard 80, or a statement on sauna use. It sits on the cool, outer side of the cedar, but ask Rockwool technical service before ordering a lot of it.

Sealing and airflow

Seal the outside against rain, and leave the inside and bottom edges able to breathe. These two goals pull in opposite directions, so each gets its own rule.

Seal the outside:

  • Lap the underlayment shingle-style (upper layer over lower) so water sheds.
  • Fit drip edge or flashing at the bottom edges.
  • Seal roof fasteners and seams, since the metal or shingles are the actual waterproofing.
  • Tuck or tape the underlayment at the ends so wind cannot blow rain up under it.

Do not seal the inside face:

  • Do not caulk or foam the cedar joints. The wood moves with heat and moisture and will crack the seal or split boards.
  • Do not put a plastic vapor barrier or foil directly on the cedar. It can trap moisture in the wood and cause rot. (The first draft suggested an optional foil layer under the insulation; that contradicts this rule, so it is dropped.)

Leave the bottom edges open:

  • Sauna heat pushes moist air through the cedar into the insulation. If every edge is sealed, that moisture condenses and soaks the mineral wool and staves, leading to mold or rot.
  • Let the roof surface and drip edge hang about 1 inch below the end of the insulation. That leaves an open pocket under the roof edge. The drip edge still sheds rain outward.
  • Cover the opening with insect screen or mesh so wasps and mice cannot move in.
  • Do the same at the two end walls: overhang 1 to 2 inches, drip edge, mesh.

Insulation product names to search for

All from Rockwool (formerly sold as Roxul):

  • Comfortboard 80: semi-rigid stone wool board, R-4.2 per inch. Thicknesses run from 1 inch up through 5 inches. Common sizes are 2 ft by 4 ft, 4 ft by 6 ft and 4 ft by 8 ft, and Rockwool’s own charts differ on which thicknesses come in which size. A Canadian retailer lists 1.5 inch as a 24 x 48 inch pack of 48 square feet (six panels) and as a 48 x 72 inch pack of 24 square feet. Check dimensions on whatever you buy; the 2 x 4 ft size is easiest to cut into strips.
  • Comfortbatt R-15: flexible batt, 3.5 inches thick, 15.25 or 23 inches wide, 47 inches long. Easy to find, but likely thicker than you want.
  • Safe’n’Sound: 3 inch batts, 15.25 or 23 inches wide, 47 inches long. Same stone wool, but sold for sound and fire rating in interior walls. It has no official R-value (forum guesses are R-11 to R-13), so it is a poor pick for this job.

Porch roof at the door

A separate freestanding porch roof, so you can dress and undress out of the rain and so weight stays off the barrel staves.

  • Size: about 4 feet deep from the door, wider than the door (about 4 to 5 feet), with room to stand, hang a towel, and maybe fit a small bench.
  • Frame: four posts: two at the front and two beside the door at the back (this fixes the first draft, which had no support at the back edge short of resting on the barrel). Put a beam across each pair and run rafters between them.
  • Slope: 3 inches of drop per foot (3:12), draining forward and away from the barrel. The first draft said 1 inch per foot, which is too flat: corrugated metal generally wants 3:12 or more, and asphalt shingles need at least 2:12 with extra underlayment at low slopes (one code summary says 4:12, so check your local code). Taller front posts or a steeper pitch also give you more headroom.
  • Height: aim for about 6 ft 8 in clear under the front edge. At 3:12 over 4 ft the back edge then ends up about 1 ft higher, which is above the top of a 6 ft barrel on its base. That is fine, because the porch then sits in front of the barrel instead of under its roof.
  • Barrel joint: keep the back edge at least 2 inches clear of the barrel and its roof overhang. Give it an upturned lip and a metal cap flashing, and do not screw anything into the staves. Measure your barrel’s height at the door end first and set the post heights from that.
  • Lumber: cedar or pressure-treated 4x4 posts, 2x6 beams and rafters, with roof material to match the barrel roof. Set posts on piers or footings suited to local frost depth and code.

Air circulation for cold feet

A heat-rated sauna fan can move air. Ordinary fans are not safe inside: motors and plastic can fail or become a fire risk at sauna temperatures. Check this section’s assumptions before buying; the first draft overstated what the fan does.

  • Product to look for: MMotors MM-S 100, a 4 inch (100 mm) sauna exhaust fan: about 105 m³/h, 16 W, IP44, rated for 140°C when running (180°C switched off) and 100% humidity, housing and back-draft damper in glass-filled polyamide. Listings include versions with a back valve. These specs come from retailer pages, not an official datasheet.
  • Where to buy: the listings I found were European sauna shops (for example esaunashop.com and orotech.lt). The first draft named Sauna Experts, Saunainter and SaunaBee, which I could not confirm. Unverified: supply voltage. EU listings are often 230 V, so find a 120 V version or a different fan before ordering.
  • Not the SaunaBox Flow: it is a cordless USB-C fan for SaunaBox models only (SmartSteam, Pulse PRO, Solara, Forge), and often sold out. Its “up to 30% more heat transfer” is a vendor claim.
  • Placement: the first draft claimed a low fan near the heater pulls warm air down along the floor. I could not find support for that. The MM-S is sold as an exhaust fan, and mounting one means cutting a 4 inch hole in a stave, which may affect your warranty. Ask Almost Heaven before cutting.
  • Try first: Almost Heaven barrels usually have a low intake vent and a high exhaust vent. If both are wide open in winter, cold air may be flooding in, so try partly closing the intake. That costs nothing.
  • Wiring: use high-temperature (silicone) wire near the fan, and have an electrician check the wiring.

Shopping list (starter)

  • Rockwool Comfortboard 80, 1.5 inch (one pack to test, then more as needed)
  • Thin furring strips or quarter-inch plywood to rip
  • About 3 inch exterior screws for the furring (pre-drill)
  • Roofing underlayment
  • Corrugated metal panels or shingles, plus drip edge
  • 1 to 1-1/4 inch roofing screws with washers, and sealant for the roof fasteners
  • Insect mesh for the open slots
  • Metal flashing and cap flashing for the porch back edge
  • Porch lumber: four posts, two beams, rafters; piers or footings
  • Dust mask, gloves and eye protection for the mineral wool
  • Optional: heat-rated sauna fan (MMotors MM-S 100, in a voltage you can use) plus high-temperature wire

Open questions

  • Heater size and circuit (confirm kW rating against your model and barrel volume, and the circuit with an electrician).
  • Barrel diameter and height at the door end, to set the porch post heights.
  • Whether the barrel’s steel hoops need notching or shimming under the furring.
  • Rockwool’s maximum service temperature for Comfortboard 80 and sauna suitability.
  • Whether Almost Heaven allows cutting a fan hole or fastening a roof without voiding the warranty.
  • Local permit rules for the porch roof and the heater circuit.

Verification notes

Checked 2026-11-04 against public pages. Confirmed items are fine as written; corrections are in the sections above.

Claim Result
Almost Heaven rain jacket, can stay on during use Confirmed (listing, archive)
Corrugated metal and shingles as roof options Confirmed in Almost Heaven’s roof blog post (archive)
Stave thickness 1-3/8 in per Almost Heaven’s Watoga page (archive); resolves the earlier open question
Comfortboard 80, 1.5 in, about R-6 R-4.2 per inch, so about R-6.3; 24 x 48 in pack of 48 sq ft listed by BMR (archive); Rockwool’s own page (archive) lists sizes differently
Comfortbatt R-15 and Safe’n’Sound sizes Confirmed (3.5 in and 3 in, 15.25 or 23 x 47 in); Safe’n’Sound has no official R-value
MMotors MM-S 100, 140°C rating Confirmed by retailers (orotech.lt, archive); it is an exhaust fan; voltage unverified
Sauna Experts, Saunainter, SaunaBee as suppliers Not confirmed; replaced
SaunaBox Flow suits a barrel Not so; it is for SaunaBox models (maker, archive)
6 kW heater typical Commonly listed on 4-person models; varies by model
Porch slope 1 in per ft Too flat; 3:12 for corrugated metal, 2:12 minimum for asphalt shingles (GAF, archive); check local code
Comfortboard 80 temperature limit in a sauna No source found; ask Rockwool
